0.title: The Kingdom of God: The Reign of God and the Hope of the World
0.essay:
Few themes in Scripture are as central, as electrifying, or as misunderstood as the kingdom of God. It is the organising theme of Jesus’ entire ministry.

Beginning and end

The first recorded words of Jesus’ preaching are, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand” (Matthew 4:17). And after his resurrection, the last subject he discussed with his disciples before ascending was the same: he appeared to them over forty days, “speaking about the kingdom of God” (Acts 1:3). The kingdom brackets his ministry from beginning to end.

Misunderstood

Yet it is one of the most debated ideas in Christian theology. Some place it entirely in the future, a political realm to be set up when Christ returns. Others collapse it entirely into the present: the church, the renewed heart, or social transformation. Still others have recruited it for political agendas of left and right alike, pressing the King into the service of causes he never endorsed.

On Jesus’ terms

This study invites us to let Jesus define his own kingdom, in his words and by his deeds. What we find is more glorious and more surprising than we expect. The kingdom is not first a territory but a reign. It is not merely future, but has already broken into history in the person of the King. It is not earned by the worthy, but given as a gift to the desperate. It is not advanced by force, but by the foolishness of proclamation. And it will not fail. It will fill the earth as the waters cover the sea.

The grammar of the Christian life

Understanding the kingdom is not an academic exercise. It is the grammar of the Christian life. Why do we pray? We are praying for the kingdom to come. Why do we suffer? Because the kingdom advances through weakness. Why do we work? Because work done for God shares in the kingdom’s forward movement. Why do we hope? Because the King is coming, and his kingdom is coming with him, in fullness and glory for ever.

The chapters

What Is the Kingdom?: the reign of God from creation to Israel. The King Has Come: Jesus and the arrival of the kingdom. Already and Not Yet: living between the ages. Kingdom Ethics: how kingdom people live. The Kingdom and the Church: the community of the King. And The Kingdom Come: new creation as the kingdom completed.

For reflection

When you pray “Your kingdom come,” what do you imagine you are asking for?

1.title: What Is the Kingdom? — The Reign of God from Creation to Israel
1.essay:
Before Jesus announced the kingdom, the kingdom already had a long history. To understand his announcement, we must hear it against Israel’s ancient, aching longing.

Creation as God’s realm

The story begins at creation. God made a world as his royal domain, installed human beings in his image as his vice-regents, and called them to rule under his sovereign reign. That was the kingdom in its original, unclouded form: the Creator ruling creation through creatures made for his glory. It was beautiful, ordered and full of his presence.

The fall and the long reclamation

The fall shattered this. Humanity seized sovereignty for itself and plunged creation into disorder, curse and death. But God did not abandon his royal purposes. He began a long work of reclamation: calling Abraham, forming Israel, giving the law, raising up kings. Israel was a kingdom-shaped people in a kingdom-shaped land, pointing towards a kingdom-shaped future.

The theme runs through every covenant. To Abraham: a great nation, a royal line and blessing for all peoples (Genesis 12:1–3). At Sinai: “you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:6). To David: a throne for ever (2 Samuel 7). In the prophets: a new covenant, a new David, the nations streaming to Zion. The whole Old Testament is one long prayer: your kingdom come.

The Lord reigns

The Psalms ring with it: “The LORD reigns; he is robed in majesty” (Psalm 93:1). At the end of his life, David prayed, “Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the victory and the majesty, for all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, O LORD, and you are exalted as head above all” (1 Chronicles 29:11).

That prayer puts Israel’s monarchy in its right place. All sovereignty belongs to the LORD. Every king of Israel was at best a steward under the greater King. And the failure of Israel’s kings was always, at root, a failure to acknowledge this.

The hope that would not die

Even in exile, when the temple burned and David’s line seemed extinct, the prophets cried that the kingdom was coming. A son of David would sit on an eternal throne. “The wolf shall dwell with the lamb” (Isaiah 11:6). “For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea” (Habakkuk 2:14). The psalms of longing — “How long, O LORD?” — were kingdom prayers, and the kingdom was the dream that kept Israel alive through the dark.

The Son of Man

Daniel saw empires as beasts: powers of force, cruelty and self-exaltation. Then: “I saw in the night visions, and behold, with the clouds of heaven there came one like a son of man, and he came to the Ancient of Days and was presented before him. And to him was given dominion and glory and a kingdom, that all peoples, nations, and languages should serve him; his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom one that shall not be destroyed” (Daniel 7:13–14).

The kingdom does not belong to the beasts. It belongs to the Son of Man, who receives it not by conquest but as the Father’s gift. Jesus would apply this vision to himself at his trial: “you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power, and coming with the clouds of heaven” (Mark 14:62). This is “a kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Hebrews 12:28).

A reign, not a territory

The Hebrew and Greek words translated “kingdom” refer first to the reign or rule of a king, not to a territory. That matters enormously. The kingdom of God is not first a place but an event: God asserting his rightful rule over what has been stolen. Wherever the King’s will is done, the kingdom is present. Wherever rebels submit to him, it expands.

That is why Jesus could say both that “the kingdom of God is in the midst of you” (Luke 17:21) and that it was still to come in power. Both are true at once, and the tension between them is the heartbeat of the Christian life.

Kingdom and gospel

Reformed theology insists that the kingdom is not an addendum to the gospel, but its setting. God’s saving work in Christ is the dramatic re-establishment of his reign over a rebel creation. Salvation is certainly the forgiveness of sins, but it is also the rescue of image-bearers for their royal calling under the true King. Herman Ridderbos, in The Coming of the Kingdom, argued that the kingdom is the central theme of Jesus’ preaching, within which justification, adoption, sanctification and new creation all find their home.

Rival kingdoms

We live among many rival kingdoms: the kingdom of self, of money, of political power, of national identity. Each demands ultimate allegiance. Each promises what only God’s kingdom can deliver. The Christian has already pledged allegiance to the true King and lives under his rule now. That is not passive waiting, but active, joyful, sometimes costly loyalty to a King who has already won.

For reflection

Which rival kingdom most competes for your allegiance? What does it mean to you that God’s kingdom is first his reign, wherever his will is done?

2.title: The King Has Come — Jesus and the In-Breaking of the Kingdom
2.essay:
When Jesus stepped out of the wilderness to preach, his first words were an announcement: the kingdom has come near. The waiting is over. The kingdom has arrived in the person of the King.

The time is fulfilled

“The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel” (Mark 1:15). Everything the Old Testament longed for finds its fullness in that moment. The kingdom is not merely approaching; it has drawn near in the one speaking these words. And the fitting response is not analysis, but repentance — a complete reorientation of life towards the King — and faith, entrusting everything to his good news.

Signs of the kingdom

Everything Jesus did must be read as kingdom activity. His healings were not only compassionate acts; they were signs of the kingdom’s arrival, foretastes of an age with no more sickness or death. His table fellowship with sinners and tax collectors was not merely countercultural; it was the kingdom banquet arriving ahead of time, open to those the religious establishment had written off.

When the Pharisees accused him of casting out demons by Beelzebul, he answered, “But if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you” (Matthew 12:28). And he explained: “no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man” (Mark 3:27). Every healing and every exorcism was the rightful King reclaiming what had been stolen. The powers of darkness were not merely losing a few battles. They were meeting their end.

The parables of the kingdom

Matthew 13 gathers Jesus’ parables of the kingdom. It is like a mustard seed, the smallest of seeds, which grows into a tree where birds nest. It is like yeast, hidden in dough until the whole is leavened (Matthew 13:31–33). Its smallness is not weakness but strategy. It grows from within, invisibly, until it cannot be contained.

“The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up. Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field” (Matthew 13:44). It is like a merchant who finds one pearl of great value and sells everything for it. The kingdom is worth everything, not as a burden, but as a joy so great that the sacrifice feels light.

And the weeds among the wheat, and the net full of good and bad fish, show that the present mixture of true and false will not last for ever. The King’s patience has an end, and his judgment will be perfect. These parables do not comfort the complacent. They call for wholehearted allegiance.

Jesus the King

The Gospels pile up royal imagery around Jesus. He enters Jerusalem on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah: “Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9). His cross bears the title “The King of the Jews,” meant as mockery but truer than Pilate knew. His resurrection is his enthronement: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matthew 28:18). His ascension is not a disappearance but a coronation. He sits at the Father’s right hand, as David foresaw: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool” (Psalm 110:1). He reigns now, invisibly but really.

The King came himself

The incarnation is the hinge of the kingdom. The kingdom arrived not as a programme or ideology, but as a person, true God and true man. The King did not send emissaries; he came himself. He did not delegate the battle; he fought it, and won. At the cross, the powers of sin and death that had usurped his rule were decisively defeated. At the resurrection, the new creation broke into the old. At the ascension, the victorious King took the throne that was always his.

So the kingdom comes wherever Jesus asserts his lordship. Every conversion is a kingdom event: another rebel lays down arms and swears allegiance. Every act of worship, every deed of obedience, every prayer “Your kingdom come,” is the reign of God being exercised through his people.

Not what they expected

The disciples expected a political king who would overthrow Rome. Instead they got a crucified King who overthrew sin and death. The kingdom came in a form so different from their expectations that they almost missed it. Only after the resurrection did they understand: this is how the King conquers, not by sword but by sacrifice, not by force but by love.

We still want a kingdom of power and comfort, one that solves our problems, restores our national fortunes and gives Christians cultural dominance. Jesus keeps offering something better: a kingdom that transforms from within, advances through witness and suffering, and does not depend on political favour or cultural approval. Every generation must decide whether to accept the kingdom on the King’s terms.

For reflection

Is the kingdom to you like treasure worth selling everything for? Where are you tempted to want a kingdom of power and comfort rather than the one Jesus offers?

3.title: Already and Not Yet — Living Between the Ages
3.essay:
The most important insight for understanding the kingdom in the New Testament is also one of the most surprising: the kingdom has come, and the kingdom is coming. Both are true at once.

Already

The kingdom has already come, in Jesus’ preaching, miracles, death, resurrection and ascension. The decisive battle has been fought and won. Satan has been defeated. Death has lost its sting. The new creation has broken in, and the Holy Spirit has been poured out as the down payment of the age to come.

“He has delivered us from the domain of darkness and transferred us to the kingdom of his beloved Son” (Colossians 1:13). The verbs are past tense: delivered, transferred. Paul is describing not a future hope but a present reality. Every Christian has already been moved from one kingdom to another, as decisively as Israel passed through the Red Sea. That transfer happened at conversion. It needs no repeating and admits no reversal.

Not yet

And yet the kingdom has not fully come. Creation still groans under the curse. Death is still the last enemy, still at work. The nations still rage. Evil is still present in the world and, most distressingly, in the hearts of God’s own people. The full harvest has not yet come. Christians still suffer, justice is still incomplete, and the wicked often seem to prosper.

“For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God” (Romans 8:19). “For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now” (Romans 8:22). This is not pessimism. It is hope set on a coming glory so weighty that present sufferings “are not worth comparing” (Romans 8:18). Every groan is a birth pang, not a death rattle.

Between D-Day and VE Day

The Christian life is lived in the space between the decisive victory and the final peace, like the months between D-Day and VE Day in 1944–45. The outcome is settled, but the fighting goes on. That is not a flaw in God’s plan. It is the very shape of the Christian life: faith, hope, endurance and longing. We live as people who know how the story ends, while still being in the middle of it.

The pattern everywhere

Once you see this pattern, you see it throughout the New Testament. We “have” eternal life (John 5:24), and we will receive it in the age to come (Mark 10:30). We have been saved (Ephesians 2:8), and “much more shall we be saved” on the last day (Romans 5:9). We have the Spirit as firstfruits (Romans 8:23), and await the full harvest. The kingdom is already present as a mustard seed, and not yet revealed as the great tree. George Eldon Ladd called this “the presence of the future”: the age to come has arrived ahead of time in Christ, but has not yet displaced the present age.

Two errors

Two errors flatten the tension. One says the kingdom is fully here now. The result is triumphalism and the prosperity gospel, the expectation that Christians should always be healthy, wealthy and winning. The other says the kingdom is entirely future. The result is escapism, a spirituality that abandons the world and simply waits for rescue.

The New Testament holds both. We fight, because the battle is real; we rest, because the victory is certain. We weep over sin and injustice, and we sing, because the King has won. We pray “Your kingdom come” with urgency, knowing that it will.

Kingdom of grace, kingdom of glory

Geerhardus Vos, Herman Ridderbos and Ladd developed this framework in the twentieth century, and it gives Christians a way to hold present grace and future hope together. The Westminster Shorter Catechism reflects the same balance, teaching us to pray that the kingdom of grace may be advanced now, and that the kingdom of glory may be hastened. Both are real, and neither is to be confused with the other.

Suffering in the overlap

This framework also helps us understand suffering. Christians do not suffer because the kingdom has failed, but because it has not yet fully come. Paul could say the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory to come because he knew where the story was going. The “already” grounds our confidence. The “not yet” sustains our hope.

The early church lived this tension sharply. They had seen the risen Lord; the kingdom had unmistakably broken in. And yet they were being persecuted, imprisoned and martyred. Revelation was written to sustain a suffering church with the vision of the coming kingdom.

Every Christian knows this tension personally. We have been forgiven, and we still sin. We have the Spirit, and we still struggle. We believe the kingdom is coming, and we watch the news and wonder. That is not immaturity. It is the normal shape of faith in the overlap of the ages. We live with one hand holding the “already” of completed salvation, and the other reaching for the “not yet” of coming glory.

For reflection

Do you lean more towards expecting too much now, or hoping too little for now? How does the “already” steady you, and the “not yet” keep you hoping?

4.title: Kingdom Ethics — How Kingdom People Live
4.essay:
If the kingdom is a present reign already breaking into the world, then kingdom people live differently, now. That is the burden of the Sermon on the Mount, the manifesto of kingdom life.

Not a ladder, but a portrait

In Matthew 5–7, Jesus is not teaching a new law by which people earn their way into the kingdom. He is describing the life that flows from those who have already received the kingdom as grace. And the more seriously we take it, the more it drives us to Christ.

Blessed are the poor in spirit

“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:3). The word for poor means destitute, bankrupt, without resources. The poor in spirit are those who know they have nothing to bring and nothing to offer. And Jesus says the kingdom is theirs. This is the paradox at the heart of the kingdom: it belongs to those who do not deserve it, and know it. The self-sufficient and the morally impressive stand outside. The desperate and the broken receive it as a gift. It is grace all the way down.

The Beatitudes that follow are a series of shocking reversals: blessed are those who mourn, the meek, the hungry for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, the persecuted. This is not a self-improvement programme. It describes people who have stopped pretending and who live from the inside out. They are declared blessed by the King himself.

A deeper righteousness

“For I tell you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5:20). The Pharisees were the most meticulous law-keepers in Israel. How could ordinary disciples exceed them? Jesus is describing a different kind of righteousness, not more of the same. Pharisaic righteousness was external, performance-based and aimed at an audience: giving, praying and fasting to be seen (Matthew 6:1–18). Kingdom righteousness is inward, driven by grace and aimed at God. It flows from a transformed heart.

You have heard… but I say

Six times Jesus says, “You have heard that it was said… But I say to you.” He is not abolishing the law; he says so plainly: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them” (Matthew 5:17). He is revealing its true intent, which was always the heart. The command against murder was always about the contempt that seeds murder. The command against adultery was always about the lust that seeds it. And the call to love reaches further than anyone imagined: “But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you” (Matthew 5:44).

Kingdom ethics are not more demanding because they add more rules, but because they go all the way down, to motive, intention and the hidden life. That makes the standard both clearer and harder, and more clearly gracious. Only Christ has fulfilled it, and only those united to him can begin to live it.

A kingdom prayer

At the centre of the Sermon is the Lord’s Prayer, a kingdom charter. “Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10). That petition frames everything else. We pray for daily bread, forgiveness and protection within the larger longing that God’s reign would extend across all of life. Everyone who prays it takes up a kingdom calling: longing for, working towards, and trusting in the full arrival of God’s rule. The prayer has never yet been answered in full. One day it will be.

The law as a map of kingdom life

Reformed theology has always insisted that the law is fulfilled, not abolished, in the kingdom. What the Reformers called the “third use” of the law — the law as a guide for Christian living — flows from this. Calvin saw the law not as a burden for believers but as a map of kingdom life: how kingdom people love God and their neighbours.

John Stott’s The Message of the Sermon on the Mount remains one of the finest expositions of kingdom ethics. He shows that the Sermon calls us neither to withdraw from the world, nor to settle comfortably into it, but to a visible, salt-and-light engagement that takes both the kingdom’s present reality and its future completion seriously.

As one who had authority

When Jesus finished, “the crowds were astonished at his teaching, for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes” (Matthew 7:28–29). He was not citing authorities; he was the authority. What he described seemed impossibly demanding and impossibly beautiful at once.

One heart at a time

Kingdom ethics are not first a programme for social transformation, though they transform societies when lived out widely. They describe what it looks like when the King rules a human heart. When a Christian forgives an enemy, prays for a persecutor, gives without fanfare, or lives with integrity in secret, these are kingdom acts. Small, often unseen, but as real as any political programme, and far more lasting.

For reflection

Which part of the Sermon on the Mount most searches your heart? Where could you show kingdom righteousness this week in a way no one else will see?

5.title: The Kingdom and the Church — The Community of the King
5.essay:
The church is not the kingdom of God. But it is the community of the kingdom. That distinction matters enormously.

Neither identical nor separate

To identify the church with the kingdom leads either to triumphalism, as if whatever the church does is kingdom activity, or to deep disillusionment when the church fails, as it always does. But to separate them entirely is equally wrong, as if the church could live its institutional life without reference to the King’s great purposes.

The church is the community of those who have entered the kingdom: who have heard the good news of the King, repented, believed, and been transferred from darkness into light. It is the firstfruits of the new humanity the kingdom will one day produce in full. And it is the primary instrument through which the kingdom advances in the world, through preaching, witness, service and love.

I will build my church

After Peter confessed Jesus as the Christ, the Son of the living God, Jesus said, “And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16:18–19).

Notice three things. First, “I will build”: the church belongs to Christ, and its existence and security are his responsibility. Second, the gates of hell will not prevail against it: many read this as the church advancing against the powers of death, rather than cowering in a fortress. Third, the keys of the kingdom: the authority, exercised through the preaching of the gospel and church discipline, to declare who is in and who is out. This is kingdom authority, delegated to kingdom servants.

Without hindrance

Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome, “proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance” (Acts 28:31). The irony is magnificent. The greatest empire on earth has imprisoned the ambassador of the only kingdom that will outlast every empire, and it cannot silence him. “The word of God is not bound!” (2 Timothy 2:9). That is the church’s calling: to keep proclaiming the kingdom until the King returns.

A kingdom-shaped community

The church’s whole identity is kingdom-shaped. Its preaching proclaims the kingdom. Its ordinances point to kingdom realities: baptism marking entry into the community of the King, and the Lord’s Supper anticipating the kingdom feast. Its discipline exercises kingdom authority. Its mission is to make disciples of all nations, bringing people under the King’s rule.

Scripture describes the church with a cluster of images: the body of Christ, under its Head; the temple of the Spirit, God’s dwelling place; the bride awaiting the wedding feast of the Lamb. And Peter applies Israel’s calling to the church: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his own possession, that you may proclaim the excellencies of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Peter 2:9). These are not descriptions of a voluntary association of religious consumers, but of a community created by grace to represent the King in the world.

Humility and freedom

The distinction between church and kingdom also brings humility. When the church fails through scandal, hypocrisy or division, the kingdom has not failed. That is sobering, because we cannot trade on the kingdom’s authority while contradicting it. And it is liberating, because the kingdom’s advance does not finally rest on our shoulders. We serve “a kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Hebrews 12:28).

The views

Rome has tended to identify the kingdom with the institutional church under the Pope. Liberal Protestantism has sometimes identified it with social transformation through political reform and moral progress. Reformed theology holds the biblical tension: the church is the community of the kingdom, its primary instrument and visible sign, but the kingdom transcends the church and will outlast every institutional form of it.

Abraham Kuyper famously declared, “There is not a square inch in the whole domain of our human existence over which Christ, who is Sovereign over all, does not cry: ‘Mine!’” The church gathers those who have acknowledged that claim. But the kingdom’s scope is the whole of creation, and the church lives and proclaims that claim in every area of life.

A colony of the kingdom

The early church understood itself as a colony of the kingdom, living by kingdom values — sharing possessions, caring for the poor, reconciling across ethnic lines — in a world organised by imperial Rome. That contrast was itself a witness.

Every local church should be a kingdom outpost. When a congregation crosses racial and economic barriers in genuine fellowship, it displays the kingdom. When it practises discipline with firmness and mercy, it exercises kingdom authority. When it sends missionaries to unreached peoples, it extends the kingdom’s frontier. When it serves the poor in its neighbourhood, it lives kingdom ethics. The question every church must ask is: do we look like a community shaped by the reign of Christ, or a slightly religious version of the surrounding culture?

For reflection

Does your church look like a colony of the kingdom? What would help it display the reign of Christ more clearly in your area?

6.title: The Kingdom Come — New Creation as Kingdom Consummated
6.essay:
The story of the kingdom does not end with the church. It ends with the King returning in glory, completing what he began, and making all things new.

Not floating souls

The Bible’s final vision is not a disembodied heaven where souls float in eternal worship. It is a new heaven and a new earth: a renewed, physical, glorified creation, full of God’s presence, free from every curse, and filled with redeemed humanity living as they were always meant to live.

It is the answer to every longing the kingdom has stirred. Creation’s groaning gives way to liberation. The tension of the already and not yet resolves into fullness. The prayer “Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven” is answered beyond anything we dared ask. The martyrs who cried, “O Sovereign Lord, holy and true, how long?” (Revelation 6:10) are vindicated.

Prepared from the foundation of the world

In the parable of the sheep and the goats, the King says, “Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34). The kingdom is not a last-minute arrangement. It was prepared in the counsels of God before creation. Its inheritance is grace all the way back. And the King is recognised in the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger and the prisoner: “as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me” (Matthew 25:40). Kingdom life always flows towards the needy, because the King himself came to the needy.

God all in all

Paul’s great resurrection chapter reaches its cosmic climax: “Then comes the end, when he delivers the kingdom to God the Father after destroying every rule and every authority and power. For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15:24–26). And the goal: “that God may be all in all” (1 Corinthians 15:28).

This is not the Son ceasing to be King, but the completion of his work as Mediator. Every rival power — sin, death, the devil, every rebel authority — has been put under his feet. The kingdom is complete and unchallenged. “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever” (Revelation 11:15).

All things new

“Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth” (Revelation 21:1). The holy city comes down out of heaven from God. “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man. He will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God” (Revelation 21:3). “He will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more” (Revelation 21:4). And the One on the throne says, “Behold, I am making all things new” (Revelation 21:5).

Not “all new things,” replacing creation with something else, but “all things new,” the renewal of what God made, loved and called very good. Heaven comes down to earth. God with us was always the destination. The incarnation was not a detour, but a foretaste.

Not a coded thriller

Revelation is not mainly a coded political thriller about ancient emperors or modern world powers. It is a sustained vision of the kingdom’s final triumph: the Lamb who was slain receiving glory, the nations streaming into the new Jerusalem, the river of life flowing from the throne, and the tree of life bearing fruit for the healing of the nations. It is Genesis completed. The garden becomes a city, filled with God’s presence, and humanity is finally conformed to the image of God’s Son.

It was written to a church under pressure, tempted to make peace with Babylon. The vision of the Lamb on the throne was not escapism. It was fuel for perseverance. Because they knew how the story would end, they could be faithful in the middle of it, even to death.

Grace restores nature

Reformed theology has stressed the physical, material nature of the completed kingdom. Anthony Hoekema’s The Bible and the Future shows that the new creation is not the destruction of the present creation but its renewal, with the same continuity as between Jesus’ body before and after his resurrection. What God made, he will redeem. Nothing good will be lost. Everything broken will be healed.

Herman Bavinck summed it up: grace restores nature. That gives our present work dignity and permanence. Paul says our labour in the Lord “is not in vain” (1 Corinthians 15:58), precisely in the context of resurrection. Faithful work done now under the King shares in something that will outlast this age.

Come, Lord Jesus

The last prayer in the Bible is the church’s oldest cry: “Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20). Paul preserved it in Aramaic, Maranatha: “Our Lord, come!” (1 Corinthians 16:22). It has been prayed by martyrs, by believers in the catacombs, by Reformers on trial, by missionaries far from home, and by the persecuted church today. It holds together the already and the not yet, the joy and the grief, the confidence and the longing.

In a world offering many rival stories — progress, national greatness, personal fulfilment — the Christian lives by the kingdom story: creation, fall, redemption, consummation. The ending is not uncertain. The King has promised it, and his resurrection guarantees it. Every Lord’s Day is a rehearsal for the final day. Until then, let us be found faithful.

For reflection

How does knowing the end of the story shape the way you live in the middle of it? Make “Come, Lord Jesus” your prayer this week.
